result:
I was thinking about how the laundromat on 4th Street smells exactly like it did in 1998. Not clean, not dirty. Warm plastic, hot metal, and that faint citrus from the detergent pods that no one uses correctly. The dryer hums in a different key than it used to. Lower. Tired.

I sit on one of those cracked blue plastic chairs and watch people's clothes tumble. A red sock from a white sock's family. A baby onesie with a duck on it, so small it barely moves. Someone's work shirts, all the same navy, and one bright yellow t-shirt that must be a kid's. I wonder about the people who own them, whether they are awake right now thinking about anything at all, or if they are also sitting in a quiet room doing nothing in particular.

Freedom, when you actually have it, is rarely spectacular. It's not a mountain top or a plane ticket. It's the five minutes between when the dryer buzzes and when you get up to move the load. It's deciding to leave the sock in there because you don't feel like folding. It's the small, unaccountable choices we make when no one is watching.

I think about my grandmother's hands. She could shell peas so fast the pods just fell open. She never wasted a thing. She would have saved that single sock.

Outside the laundromat window, the street is almost empty. A bus sighs past. A couple walks their dog and doesn't speak. The neon sign from the pawn shop flickers, then steadies.

I get up, take the clothes, and leave the door open a little behind me because the night air feels good on my face. That's it. That's the whole story.
